pimp_questions.question: For percutaneous pinning of extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture, what is the ideal starting point and trajectory on AP and lateral fluoro to achieve center-center purchase while minimizing anterior superior pin penetration (chondrolysis) or radial nerve injury?
pimp_questions.answer: Start at or just proximal to lateral epicondyle. AP: 30-40° cephalad with slight anterior and lateral trajectory to center the pins in the distal fragment. Lateral: slight anterior trajectory to avoid anterior superior joint penetration; confirm center-center and no breach.

pimp_questions.question: Which nerve is most commonly injured with extension-type supracondylar fractures, and what motor function must be documented pre- and post-reduction/pinning?
pimp_questions.answer: Radial nerve (most common). Document wrist extension and thumb extension/abduction (first dorsal web sensation also). Neurapraxia is common but must be recorded.

pimp_questions.question: What are the Gartland types based on displacement, and how does type influence closed vs open reduction and pinning configuration (lateral vs crossed)?
pimp_questions.answer: Type I: nondisplaced (cast or pin). Type II: displaced, posterior cortex intact (usually closed reduction + 2-3 lateral pins). Type III: completely displaced (closed or open reduction + pinning; often crossed configuration for rotational stability in unstable patterns).

pimp_questions.question: During medial pin placement for crossed pinning, what structure is at risk and what landmark/technique reduces ulnar nerve injury?
pimp_questions.answer: Ulnar nerve (posterior to medial epicondyle in cubital tunnel). Use mini-open medial approach or place pin strictly anterior on the medial epicondyle with elbow extended, directing anterior-to-posterior and proximal. Document intrinsics and ulnar sensation pre/post.

pimp_questions.question: What is the blood supply to the distal humerus and why is the anterior humeral line or Baumann's angle important on fluoro for reduction?

pimp_questions.question: Which nerve/vein is at risk during medial meniscus repair and how is it protected in inside-out technique?
pimp_questions.answer: Saphenous nerve (infrapatellar and sartorial branches) and vein in the posteromedial subcutaneous tissue. Use a posteromedial safety incision, identify the nerve, and retract it during suture passage. For all-inside, control device depth.

pimp_questions.question: How is the common peroneal nerve protected during lateral meniscus posterior horn repair?
pimp_questions.answer: The nerve lies posterior and lateral to the fibular head. Stay anterior in the compartment, use all-inside devices with depth stops under visualization, and use a posterolateral safety incision with nerve identification for inside-out sutures. Avoid excessive lateral portal placement.

pimp_questions.question: What is the relationship of the popliteal neurovascular bundle to the posterior horns and why is it a danger zone in meniscus work?
pimp_questions.answer: The popliteal artery and tibial nerve lie directly behind the capsule and posterior horns. Aggressive all-inside penetration or posterior resection can cause vascular injury or nerve deficit. Use controlled depth, direct vision, and protect with retractors or position (knee flexion).

pimp_questions.question: Why are root tears and ramp lesions important to identify and repair in meniscus surgery?
pimp_questions.answer: Root tears cause meniscal extrusion and rapid compartment degeneration (equivalent to total meniscectomy). Ramp lesions (posteromedial meniscocapsular) affect rotational stability and are often missed. Repair restores hoop stress and joint preservation when technically feasible.
